PART 5 — LOVE, BOUNDARIES AND EXPLOITATION

5.1 Sacrifice Versus Being Used

Sacrificial loveExploitation
Who choosesYou, freely (John 10:18)Someone takes, often via guilt, fear or authority
Your "no"RespectedIgnored or punished
Described asA giftA duty, "God's will," "just how it is"
Effect on youMeaningful, even costlyDrained, resentful, smaller

Signs of exploitation: repeated one-sided taking beyond what was agreed; your "no" ignored or punished; being valued mainly for what you provide; guilt, fear or spiritual pressure used to get compliance.

5.2 What Scripture Actually Says (Correcting Common Misreadings)

Common beliefWhat Scripture says
"Love bears all things, so endure it."1 Cor 13:6-7: love "does not rejoice at wrongdoing but rejoices with the truth." Paul rebukes a church for tolerating exploitation (2 Cor 11:20).
"Turn the other cheek."Matt 5:39 forbids retaliation in kind; Jesus himself questioned being struck (John 18:23) — he confronted, did not simply absorb.
"Never confront; just pray."Matt 18:15-17 gives a path: alone, then witnesses, then the church. Eph 4:15,25: speak truth in love.
"Suffering is Christian."1 Pet 2:18-21 addresses those without power to leave. "If you can gain your freedom, avail yourself of it" (1 Cor 7:21); Gal 5:1.
"Always submit to leaders."Acts 5:29. Leaders are not to dominate (1 Pet 5:2-3; Matt 20:25-28); God opposes shepherds who feed on the flock (Ezek 34:2-4).
"Forgive means pretend it didn't happen."Forgiveness releases a debt; it is not restored trust. Luke 17:3-4 pairs rebuke with repentance.
"Keep the peace at any cost."Jer 6:14 condemns false peace. Rom 12:18: "so far as it depends on you." Prov 29:25; Gal 1:10.
"Do not judge."Matt 7:1-5 forbids hypocritical, contemptuous judgment — not naming wrong or setting limits (Matt 18:15; 1 Cor 5:12-13).

Wages and work: Scripture is direct about worker exploitation — Lev 19:13; Deut 24:14-15; James 5:4 (withheld wages "cry out"); Col 4:1.

5.3 The Root: Why Enduring Feels Like Love

I-AM-NOT: "I am not wanted, important, worthy unless useful"
↓
BELIEF: "Love is earned by being useful; conflict costs me love"
↓
METHODS: self-salvation, confirmation, fix-me, numbing (Kruger's 1, 5, 4, 2)
↓
BEHAVIOR: silence, over-giving, appeasing, "it's fine," resentment
↓
OUTCOME: exploitation continues; exhaustion

This is the Seeker pattern from Part 1.4, applied specifically to being used. The body's survival pattern (a learned "fawn" response) makes speaking up feel unsafe, not just uncomfortable — which is exactly what the Voice Ladder (Part 4.1) is built to retrain. The person exploiting is responsible for the exploitation; this explains why speaking up is hard, it does not blame the person being used.

Would you meet this week?"Written record → manager → HR/senior manager → outside/legal advice for pay issues

Would you share or rotate the others?"Elders/senior leader → denominational or outside leader if a leader is dominating (Ezek 34; 1 Pet 5:3)

Safety first. If there is violence, threats, sexual abuse, serious coercion or control, do not attempt an NVC conversation alone. Prioritize safety, a trusted person, and professional/official help. NVC is for situations where speaking honestly is safe enough.

A four-question test for any act of "love": Is it free? Is it truthful? Does it seek the good of everyone, including the person taking advantage? Is there mutuality over time?

5.6 Self-Love, Lovers of Self, and "Deny Yourself" — Untangled

PhraseWhat it meansWhat it does NOT mean
"Deny yourself" (Luke 9:23)Surrendering the self that rules, protects and promotes itself — the ego's need for approval, revenge, status (Gal 2:20)Denying your worth, voice, needs, body or personhood
"Love your neighbour as yourself" (Mark 12:31)Assumes you rightly care for yourself (Eph 5:29)That you must love others while despising yourself
"Lovers of self" (2 Tim 3:2)Self-absorbed, boastful, using others — the Defender's faceHealthy self-care or self-respect

Healthy self-love is not self-esteem you generate (see Part 1.7) — it is receiving the Father's love ("We love because he first loved us," 1 John 4:19) so you can treat yourself and others with truth, care and limits. Dying to self means saying no to the ego's demand to be liked by everyone, so you can say yes to real love. For the exploited person, the "self" to deny is the fear and the need for approval — never their dignity.

6.3 Why Church Culture Sometimes Builds Self-Neglect

This analysis of institutional and theological causes is the source document's own synthesis.

  1. Real history becomes a template. Missionary/persecution stories (Acts 5:41; Heb 11) are honourable; the problem is when costly calling under persecution becomes the norm for ordinary life.
  2. Texts read without context — "deny yourself," "living sacrifice," household codes used to justify self-erasure (fuller reading in Part 5.6).
  3. Suspicion of the self and body. Paul calls severity to the body "of no value" (Col 2:20-23); the body is a temple (1 Cor 6:19-20).
  4. Institutional incentives — volunteer-run organizations benefit from limitless sacrifice; God condemns shepherds who feed on the flock (Ezek 34:2-4).
  5. I-am-nots at scale — sacrifice becomes the currency of worth; Seekers over-give, some Defenders gain status from others' giving.
  6. Confusing the cross with suffering itself. Jesus chose his sacrifice (John 10:18), rested (Mark 6:31), said "I desire mercy, not sacrifice" (Matt 9:13).
HealthyExploitative
GivingVoluntary, mutual, transparentGuilt- or fear-driven; secretive
RestBuilt in, modeled by leadersAbsent; burnout everywhere
Saying noPossible without penaltyTreated as rebellion or lack of faith
QuestionsWelcomed (Acts 17:11)Shamed or punished

6.4 Called to Love Everyone, Yet Not Everyone's Savior

Everyone — pray, goodwill, justiceNeighbours you meet — mercy as ableYour community — serve within limitsYour household — first practical responsibilityYourself — the steward who must stay well

Only God can be everything to everyone. Jesus lived this limit: he left crowds to pray and moved on ("that is why I came," Mark 1:35-38); healed one man among many at Bethesda (John 5:3-9); "did not entrust himself to everyone" (John 2:24); chose a few to invest in deeply rather than equally in all (Luke 6:13); did not stop Mary to make her serve (Luke 10:38-42); rested (Mark 4:38; 6:31). The Good Samaritan helped the one he met, paid the innkeeper, and continued his journey — he did not stay forever or rescue the whole road (Luke 10:35). Moses was warned by Jethro: "you will wear yourself out" — delegate (Ex 18:17-23). The apostles refused to drop their calling to wait tables (Acts 6:2-4). Paul worked within "the area of influence God assigned," not beyond it (2 Cor 10:13).

6.6 Answering Accusations When You Set a Boundary

What people sayWhat's happeningA calm response
"If you really loved me, you would..."Love used as leverage (guilt)"I do love you, and my answer is still no."
"Are you even a Christian?"Identity attacked to force compliance"I follow Christ and have prayed about this. We may see it differently."
"You abandoned your parents."Distance equated with neglect"I am not leaving you. I will visit, help and stay in touch."
"What will people say? Our testimony!"Reputation used as authority"I care about our witness. I live by integrity, not by opinions."
"The pastor/elders say you must."Authority pressure"I will pray and seek counsel; the decision is mine before God."

How to hold the line: acknowledge their feeling; affirm your love; state your decision; offer what you can do; repeat calmly; do not over-explain. If it escalates, pause, keep contact, involve a trusted outside person.

6.7 Family and Culture: Honoring Parents, Moving Out, Testimony

Both are true: caring for parents is a real duty (1 Tim 5:4,8; John 19:26-27), and marriage forms a new household ("a man shall leave his father and mother," Gen 2:24, quoted by Jesus in Matt 19:5). Moving out is not abandonment. "Honour" (addressed to adults, Ex 20:12) is not the same as "obey" (addressed to children, Eph 6:1); loyalty to Christ comes first (Matt 10:37).

RESPECT — speak kindly, listenREGULAR CONTACT — calls, visitsREAL HELP WITHIN LIMITSRIGHT TO DECIDE — home, marriage, career, faith

What "testimony" really means: a life of integrity (Matt 5:16; 1 Pet 2:12), not a public image controlled by others' opinions. Jesus was criticized and kept going ("a glutton and a drunkard," Matt 11:19); he "did not receive glory from people" (John 5:41). "It is a very small thing to be judged by you" (1 Cor 4:3). The gospel answers shame directly: Jesus "despised the shame" (Heb 12:2) — in an honour-shame culture, the Father's verdict is the honour that counts (connects directly to Part 3's whole treatment of shame).

6.8 Is Self-Care Selfish?

SelfishSelf-care
AimMy benefit at others' expenseStaying well so I can love well
Others' needsIgnoredIncluded; met within capacity
TestDoes it harm others' real needs?Does it help me love better over time without harming others?

Jesus rested (Mark 6:31; Luke 5:16); Elijah was sent sleep and food before work (1 Kgs 19:5-8); "He gives to his beloved sleep" (Ps 127:2); Moses was warned he'd wear himself out (Ex 18:18); "no one hates his own flesh but nourishes it" (Eph 5:29). Rules of balance: separate duty from demand; capacity first (2 Cor 8:12); give freely, not under compulsion (2 Cor 9:7); honour without obedience; seek outside counsel (Prov 11:14); expect pushback and stay steady; rest as obedience, not a lack of it.
